name: Peter Yi Ho-yong
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Execution dates are not treated as feast days; a shared celebration requires a scoped calendar citation.
biography: Peter Yi Ho-yong was born in Incheon and later lived in poverty with his family in Seoul. He learned the Catholic faith from Paul Yi Kyong-on and became a catechist after the arrival of the Chinese priest Pacificus Yu. His older sister, Agatha Yi So-sa, also helped sustain the family and its religious life.

Arrested in 1835, Peter continued to pray and instruct others during a long imprisonment. He and Agatha sometimes met under guard and encouraged each other. Illness and the harsh conditions weakened him, and he died in prison in 1838. The Korean bishops identify him among the 103 canonized martyr saints.

name: Protasius Chong Kuk-bo
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Execution dates are not treated as feast days; a shared celebration requires a scoped calendar citation.
biography: Protasius Chong Kuk-bo worked with his father making straw rope in Seoul after the family lost its former prosperity. He encountered Catholicism as an adult. A priest entrusted him with a house where Catholics visiting the capital could stay while receiving the sacraments, and Protasius and his wife cared for these guests.

During the 1839 persecution he initially renounced his faith under pressure and was released. He regretted that decision and repeatedly sought permission to retract it before the authorities. Returned to prison, he suffered further beatings and illness and died there in May. His biography emphasizes repentance as well as his final perseverance.

name: Agatha Kim A-gi
feast_note: A Catholic liturgical calendar date has not yet been verified for this entry. Execution dates are not treated as feast days; a shared celebration requires a scoped calendar citation.
biography: Agatha Kim A-gi came from a household without Catholic ties and married into another such family. A visit from her Catholic older sister prompted her to study the faith. She struggled to memorize prayers, but continued her preparation despite the danger that becoming Catholic brought in Korea at that time.

She was arrested in 1836 and received baptism while imprisoned. Alongside Magdalene Kim Ob-i and Barbara Han A-gi, she refused demands to renounce her belief. After years in confinement, Agatha was executed in Seoul in 1839. The bishops' account records her canonization in 1984; it does not establish a modern medical diagnosis for her learning difficulties.

biography: Anna Pak A-gi grew up in a Catholic family near the Han River. She married, raised five children and taught them the faith, drawing particular strength from prayer about Christ's Passion. She was arrested with her husband and eldest son in 1836.

Her husband and son renounced their faith and were released, but Anna remained in prison. Their repeated appeals for her to return home added to the distress of imprisonment and torture. biography: Magdalene Kim Ob-i practiced Catholicism from childhood. Although she had hoped to remain unmarried, she accepted her parents' decision that she should marry. biography: Augustine Yi Kwang-hon became Catholic as an adult after a conversation that led him to reconsider his earlier conduct. biography: Lucia Pak Hui-sun served as a lady-in-waiting in the Korean royal palace and could read both Korean and Chinese. After learning about Catholicism, she obtained permission to leave court life. Her father opposed her conversion, so she lived with a nephew rather than returning to the family home.

biography: Damian Nam Myong-hyok became Catholic around the age of thirty and received baptism from the priest Pacificus Yu. As a catechist, he taught in his home and cared for sick neighbors. He also kept religious items belonging to Bishop Laurent Imbert.

biography: Joseph Chang Song-jip worked in a herb shop in Seoul and was twice widowed. He began studying Catholicism as an adult but stopped when he struggled with its teachings about the Incarnation and Christ's birth. A Catholic friend later persuaded him to resume his religious life.

Joseph turned to prayer, meditation and Scripture, and received baptism and confirmation in 1838. Arrested during the following year's persecution, he explained his beliefs to those urging him to abandon them. After beatings and continued imprisonment, he died in a Seoul prison in May 1839. The Korean bishops include him among their canonized martyrs.

biography: Barbara Kim came from a poor Catholic household and entered domestic service while young. Living with a devout Catholic family strengthened her religious commitment. She later married a man who did not share her faith, and differences over religion troubled their family life.

biography: Barbara Yi was an orphan from Seoul who lived with her aunts, Magdalene Yi Yong-hui and Barbara Yi Chong-hui. The Korean bishops' account describes her as a young teenager at the time of her arrest. She continued to profess her faith when questioned and tortured by the authorities.

biography: John Baptist Yi Kwang-nyol embraced Catholicism with his older brother Augustine Yi Kwang-hon. He traveled to Beijing, where he was baptized. On returning to Korea he chose an unmarried life marked by prayer and religious discipline.

biography: John Pak Hu-jae was born in Yongin and later earned a living making straw shoes in Seoul. His father, Laurence Pak, had died for the faith during the earlier persecution. John married and practiced Catholicism while supporting his household through his trade.

biography: Augustine Yu Chin-gil was an interpreter whose religious inquiry led him from reading Korean and Chinese philosophical traditions to Catholic writings. biography: Sebastian Nam I-gwan came from a family affected by the 1801 persecution, when his father died in exile. Sebastian himself spent years in exile and received baptism as an adult. biography: Ignatius Kim Che-jun was the father of Andrew Kim Tae-gon, who became Korea's first native Catholic priest. Ignatius supported the decision to send Andrew to Macao for priestly studies, despite the danger that sending him abroad created for the family.

biography: Perpetua Hong Kum-ju grew up with her grandmother and married while young. After losing her husband and later her son, she lived in Minari-kol. A Catholic householder helped her renew her understanding of the catechism, and she became known for prayer and practical service to others.

biography: Cecilia Yu So-sa became Catholic through her husband, Augustine Chong Yak-jong. After his martyrdom in 1801, she and her children faced confiscation of their property and a difficult period living with relatives. Her son Paul Chong Ha-sang later helped bring missionaries into Korea.

biography: Barbara Cho Chung-i was married to Sebastian Nam I-gwan. The earlier persecution separated them when he was exiled, and she eventually moved to Seoul to live among practicing Catholics. biography: Magdalene Han Yong-i was married to Kwon Chin, a government official who became Catholic in middle age. He encouraged her to embrace the faith and, before dying, asked her to continue practicing it. Magdalene then lived in poverty while maintaining her religious commitment.
